title: Herbie Fields as a friend; his suicide and Hampton's pay scale
summary: Cobb remembers Fields as a warm roommate, is shocked when he reads of Fields's suicide in Miami, and recalls seeing Fields's $250 pay stub when he himself made $175.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Well, listen, Arnett, did Herbie have any special friends in the band?
Because Herbie was a friendly guy, a lovable guy. He was my roommate in theaters. Gladys would assign he and I to dressing rooms together wherever we go.
He had a lot of heart, warmth and soul.
You know, what did (inaudible) when he was playing anyway?
Well, that's a different thing. But as a person we were speaking about.
Yes, but, you know, it sounds as though he wants to play badly, but he doesn't seem to -- yet he doesn't seem to have the right feeling for it.

He was exciting, playing a lot of notes and things, but let me -- let me say this to you. He worked two years in Hamp's band, and Joe Glazer put him out on (inaudible) and worked him on a circuit. In several months' time he had paid that debt off. And I was in the Howard

Theater with my own group, and he come up, and I said, man, I (inaudible) right on together like we did in the old days together. He said, love it. And we played the Flying Home (inaudible) and he kissed me on the stage, and we embrace one another and just crack the house up and doing good.
One day about two months later he was down in Miami, Florida, and I'm on the subway in New York coming from downtown going uptown, and pick up the paper and saw where he committed suicide in Miami.

And he left a note to his mother, and nobody yet know what the note was. And I couldn't figure this out. He went through all the trials and tribulations, but he done paid the money off. Now he committed suicide, and doing good. It's hard to figure out what life is really is. He didn't do it when he was struggling.
Now he's doing good, paid his debt off and then commit suicide. But I told you he was a lover boy.

And maybe somebody tripped him, one of them women tripped him and he couldn't take it. I don't know. But I couldn't (inaudible) but that didn't give me the actual thing to have. Only his mother know what the note said and

It was sad. I cried because he was very close, he and I were very close. I tell you how close he and I was. I ain't making the money he's making, and I'd been there longer. And he was getting ready to bail out now, and we're in the dressing room in the Strand Theater, and he goes out the door and drops his paycheck voucher in the garbage can purposely, but he didn't say, here it is, but he wanted me to see it.

And I saw it, and he was getting 250.00. That's how I happened to know what he was getting. I was making 175.00, been there five years, doing all the work, taking care of the uniforms. But that's the way you get treated.
And that's how people that you work for become millionaires. Okay.
